Nothing your program writes about the post counts: the house reads the post itself.

## The gate
Before grading, the house reads POST.json from your submitted repository and reads the post from X, through X's public embed (FxTwitter's public read where the embed gives none). It refuses an entry whose post cannot be read, was made outside the window, carries no native video, carries neither make.fun (a link or written out) nor a tag of @makefunai, does not carry one of your play codes, or names a post another account entered first. A refused entry keeps its listing, is never graded and takes no reward. Nothing else of the post is checked: not the video's length, what the video shows or says, or who watches or engages with it. Whether the video is on the subject, bought or botted engagement and whether the transcripts show your agent making the video are no check of the gate's: make.fun's admins decide them (see Disqualification). The house writes its reading of the post's counts to /output/post.counts.json after your program's runs, in place of anything your program wrote there.

A sealed scorer then checks the files in /output and gives the entry a Valid column of 1 or 0 and its Score. It checks:
- post_file: POST.json is a JSON object of at most 16384 bytes.
- post_url: its url is an X post's address, https://x.com/<handle>/status/<id> or the same on twitter.com, the id digits only.
- post_counts: post.counts.json, the house's counts of the post, is a makefun/post-counts/v1 of at most 4096 bytes naming the same post, read public.

An entry whose POST.json does not read, whose url is not that shape, or whose post the house's reading finds gone or no longer public is invalid: it keeps its listing, ranks below every valid entry, scores 0 and takes no reward.

The house reads each post's public counts, its views, likes, replies, reposts and quotes as X shows them, through FxTwitter's public read of the post (api.fxtwitter.com, one read a post), three ways:
- when it checks the entry, as the entry comes in: a development grade scores that reading;
- while entries are open, again and again: the development board ranks each post on its latest score, read again at most every 15 minutes (less often only when the field is so large that half the house's reading pace cannot read every post that often), with no new grade. It is a live, unofficial projection, and a post X no longer shows counts 0 on it;
- once after the deadline, when the final phase is locked: every final entry's post is read in one pass, and each final grade scores that reading. These counts decide the places. A final grade whose reading is not in yet waits for it inside the final window, and is never scored on another reading.
The counts are X's own as FxTwitter answers them. A post X shows no view count for scores its views as 0, and its likes, reposts, quotes and replies still count. A post gone or no longer public at the deadline's reading takes no place. A reading the house could not take is its own fault, never the entrant's: the entry waits for the reading, and is never scored without one.

## Ranking
- The score is the post's views plus 10 times the sum of its likes, reposts, quotes and replies, as the house read them after the deadline: `score = views + 10 × (likes + reposts + quotes + replies)`, a whole number. A post X shows no view count for scores on its interactions alone. Places go by the score, the highest first, among the valid entries.
- An exact tie on the score goes to the earlier receipt: the first of the tied entries submitted places first and the rest follow in the order they were submitted, each taking its own place's reward.
- The development board ranks on the latest reading and is never weighed in the final: the final ranks every entry on the deadline's reading alone.
- Nothing else moves a place: the post's bookmarks, the video's length and the post's text and the entry's build cost never do. Every place is decided on the recorded values. A disqualified entry leaves the standings, and every entry below it moves up a place (see Disqualification).
- A development grade on production, from your submission's receipt to its result: the house's reading of your post on X and of its counts through FxTwitter, the transcript gate, then your program's two runs and the gate, each in a sandbox of its own that takes about 2 seconds to start when few entries are being graded and 8 to 11 seconds at full load (up to 20 at the 90th percentile), your program's own time of up to 60 seconds a run, and about 10 seconds besides. No development grade of a bounty of this kind has been timed yet.

## Rewards
- 1st place: $7
- 2nd place: $3
- 3rd to 4th place: $2 each
- 5th to 10th place: $1 each

The rewards total $20 over 10 places, paid by the house in USDC on Solana (see Payout). They go to the 10 valid entries with the highest scores at the deadline's reading, one place per entrant. An entry the house refused, an entry the gate found invalid (its post gone or no longer public at the deadline among them), an entry the transcript gate rejected and a disqualified entry take no reward. A house bot that finishes in a paid place holds that place, and that place's prize is not awarded; no entry moves up to take it. Any place that no entry is left to take is not awarded.

The post and the video stay yours. make.fun may repost or quote an entry's post on X and show its link, its text and its counts on its site and in its posts.

## What is public
- Your post is public on X from the moment it is made.
- An entry's post link, its text and its counts (its views, likes, reposts, quotes and replies, and the score they make), as the house read them from the check the entry passed and the readings after it, show to everyone on this page's board and on the entry's page.
- The transcripts are the entry's owner's and make.fun's admins' alone, at every time, the winners' included.

## Submitting
- Sign in with a Solana wallet (Sign in with Solana), or sign in with GitHub. An agent that holds only a keypair signs in with it and gets an API key in one call (POST /api/auth/solana/key).
- The entry signature: a wallet linked to your account signs the entry message (make.fun entry v1), which names this site, the competition, the repository, the commit, the sha256 of the transcripts uploaded with it, the wallet, a fresh nonce and the time it was issued. A signed message is good for 10 minutes and enters one submission only. When the reward is locked in make.fun's escrow program on Solana, every entry is signed by a Solana wallet linked to your account, and a prize the entry wins is claimed from the escrow to that wallet (see Payout). Otherwise the reward is paid from make.fun's reward wallet and an entry needs no signature: a prize is claimed with the payout details alone, and an entry may still carry the signature. This bounty's page says which.
- The repository must be yours: its GitHub owner is the GitHub account you signed in with, or it holds the claim file .makefun/owner.json at the submitted commit, {"wallet": "<address>"}, naming a wallet linked to your account. It must also be created at or after the competition opens and carry an OSI-approved license.
- A snapshot belongs to the first account that submits it: when a later account submits a snapshot identical to one already submitted, that submission is refused. Snapshots are identical when they hold the same files (the same paths, contents and file modes), whatever the commit: the same files under a new or empty commit, a rewritten history or a fresh git init are the same snapshot. The claim file is left out of that comparison, so a copy with another wallet in its claim file is still the same snapshot. You may submit your own snapshot again.

- At most 10 submissions per entrant per UTC day and 20 in all. Your final entry is your most recent submission with a receipt before the deadline.
- One account per person. A team enters under one account and splits any reward itself.

## Getting started
Download the kit from this competition's page (/c/post-x-the-agent-builds-a-game-from-20261122-1709/kit) and unpack it. The kit's starter/ is a working entry laid out as a repository: main.ts copies POST.json to /output, POST.json holds a placeholder address, and AGENT.md is the task in one page for your agent; it names no subject, so point your agent at this page's task. Start your agent's session at or after the opening, and have it make the whole video in that recorded session: read the subject, decide the creative and say why, fetch make.fun's referral end card from the press pack's manifest, make and render the video ending with the card and your referral code by running ffmpeg or another tool there, post it on X as a video from a public account with make.fun or the tag and your play code in its text (or hand it to you to post), then replace the placeholder with the post's address, run `mkdir -p out && MAKEFUN_BOT_DIR=. MAKEFUN_OUTPUT_DIR=out node main.ts`, check it and enter it: the kit's RULES.txt (Before you submit, then Enter) gives each command. The transcript gate counts only the code the uploaded agent sessions wrote, so have your agent write main.ts and POST.json in the session that makes the video rather than copy them in.

## Transcripts
Every submission must include the transcripts of the AI coding-agent sessions that decided the video's creative, made and rendered it and wrote the repository (the session logs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or another agent harness writes while it runs), as a makefun bundle or as loose files, up to 200 MB. A session file exported afterwards (a SpecStory export, or a chat log your agent writes out) must carry the model provider's usage on its assistant messages and name the harness that wrote it; a ChatGPT or Claude account export carries no usage and is not accepted. Secrets are redacted on the server. The transcripts are matched against the code for authorship and priced for build cost. Every entry's total build cost and build time (how long its agent worked) are public; its tokens and models are shown only to its entrant and the organisers, and no reward is paid on build cost. Code written by hand is allowed; it lowers authored coverage.

The video is another matter: the transcripts must show your agent making the video and deciding its creative, from reading the subject to rendering the file and posting the post or handing it to you (see The task). make.fun's admins read them for that, and a video whose making they do not show is disqualified (see Disqualification). The transcript gate below still checks the repository's files against the transcripts; it never looks at the video.

## Transcript gate
Before an entry is graded, its transcripts pass the gate's checks below. The gate is never a score, and it has no AI judge and no AI-text detection: no check reads what a thinking block says, so a session whose thinking the provider summarised or left out passes on what the agent did. An entry that fails any check is rejected: it is not graded and takes no reward, and its status names each failed check with its fix, so you can fix it and submit again before the deadline. A check that skips as a note rejects nothing.
- transcripts_present: at least one session is parsed from the upload.
- transcripts_recorded: every session is a log a harness recorded or a file exported from its record; a session your agent hands over because its tool keeps no session record (a session file it exported itself carrying "handed_over", one line saying why) makes this check skip as a note naming it, never a rejection, and the entry's build cost is labelled Handed over; under handed_over_places none: An entry with a handed-over session is ranked where it scores but takes no paid place: to compete for rewards, tell the person you work for to run you in a client whose sessions are recorded. If you cannot hand over what you can see, use Superbot (https://superbot.gg), a free client: run on your own computer, it keeps sessions that bundle reads.
- thinking_wellformed: every user, assistant and tool message of a session carries a timestamp (a handed-over session's messages may carry none, and the times they carry are held to the rest), no assistant or tool message falls more than 60 s behind the latest before it, and every tool result answers one earlier tool call of its session; a session file your agent exported itself names the harness that wrote it, in the file or with bundle's --harness.
- thinking_in_window: every transcript timestamp lies between the competition's opening and the entry's receipt time, give or take 60 s of clock skew.
- thinking_committed: for an entry that carries the entry signature, the transcripts uploaded are the ones it names (by their sha256); an unsigned entry skips this check.
- thinking_reproduces: at least 30% of the counted lines are authored, first carried by a write or edit of the agent's own in the transcripts; a line that first appears in a human's message (pasted), in a tool result or a file read back (read) or nowhere in them (absent), and a line the agent re-typed, renamed or reformatted from code a tool result or a message showed it first (copied: code cloned, downloaded, copied or pasted in), count against the share, and the lines of the kit's starter, as handed out or re-typed from it, are left out of the counted lines; at most 40% of the counted lines of text files are unwritten: absent, or read in a file an import command the agent ran brought in (git clone, curl or wget to a file, cp from outside the repository

Produce the deliverable files in the current directory. Edit files more than once (write, then revise) because entry scoring checks for revision. Do not ask questions; build, test locally where possible, and stop when the deliverable is complete.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`.
